reading.title: The Mapmaker of the Hills
paras: Long before modern satellites could photograph the earth, a young woman named Naina Rawat was already drawing careful maps of the hills around her home in Uttarakhand. Born in 1942 in a remote mountain village, Naina grew up watching her father guide travellers along narrow forest paths. He was a postman who walked for miles each day, carrying letters across streams and steep slopes, and Naina often followed him on holidays.

As a child, Naina was fascinated by the shapes of rivers, ridges and valleys. She would collect stones, leaves and bits of charcoal, and use them to sketch the land on the ground outside her house. Her teachers at the village school noticed her talent and encouraged her to study geography. Although books were scarce, Naina borrowed whatever she could find and spent her evenings reading by the light of an oil lamp.

After completing her studies in Dehradun, Naina joined a government survey team. At that time, very few women worked in field surveying, and many people doubted whether she could manage the difficult mountain terrain. Naina proved them wrong through determination and patience. She walked long distances, climbed rocky paths and recorded every detail with accuracy.

Over the years, Naina helped prepare maps that were later used to build roads, schools and health centres in remote areas. Her work made it easier for villagers to receive supplies during harsh winters and for rescue teams to reach people during landslides. She believed that a good map was not merely a drawing, but a tool that could save lives.

Even after her retirement, Naina continued to teach young students how to observe nature closely. She reminded them that the land always tells a story, and that those who learn to read it carefully can serve their communities in remarkable ways. Today, many young surveyors in the region still speak of her with respect and gratitude.

reading.title: The Night the River Rose
paras: It had been raining without pause for three days in the riverside town of Dharapur. The sky remained a dull grey, and the sound of water filled every street. At first, people were not worried because the monsoon often brought heavy showers. But by the evening of the third day, the river began to swell, creeping closer to the rows of small houses along its bank.

Aarav, a Class VIII student, noticed the danger when he saw muddy water slipping into the lane behind his home. He remembered the safety drill his school had conducted earlier that year. Instead of panicking, he urged his family to gather important papers, medicines and a torch, and to move to the community hall on higher ground.

As they stepped out, Aarav saw that some neighbours were still inside their houses, unsure of what to do. He called out to them and explained that the water level was rising quickly. Together with a few older boys, he helped an elderly couple carry their bags and guided two small children through the flooded lane.

By midnight, dozens of families had taken shelter in the hall. Volunteers distributed dry food and blankets, while teachers from the local school kept a list of everyone who had arrived. The rain continued to fall, but there was a sense of calm because people were looking out for one another.

Two days later, the water slowly receded, leaving behind mud and broken fences. Cleaning the town took time and effort, yet the residents felt grateful that no lives had been lost. Aarav realised that courage was not always loud or dramatic; sometimes it was simply the decision to stay alert and help others at the right moment.

reading.title: A Library on Wheels
paras: In several dusty villages of Rajasthan, where the nearest town library is many kilometres away, a bright blue bus arrives every Saturday morning. Painted with pictures of open books and smiling children, the bus is known as the Mobile Pathshala. It carries more than two thousand books, a small computer, and a cheerful librarian named Farida Begum.

Farida started the travelling library in 2015 after noticing that many children in her district loved stories but had very little to read. Her own childhood had been shaped by books borrowed from a neighbour, and she wanted to give other children the same chance. With support from a local education group, she converted an old bus into a moving library.

Inside the bus, shelves are neatly arranged by age and subject. There are picture books for younger children, adventure stories for older readers, and reference books for students preparing for exams. Farida also keeps a box of puzzles and magazines, because she believes that reading should feel joyful rather than forced.

The Mobile Pathshala does more than lend books. Farida reads aloud to small groups, helps children choose books that match their interests, and encourages them to return the following week to share what they have read. For many families, Saturday has become the most eagerly awaited day of the week.

Over the years, the bus has inspired several children to write their own stories and poems. Some have even started small reading corners in their homes. Farida says that a library does not always need tall walls and silent rooms; sometimes, all it needs is wheels and a willing heart.

reading.title: The Weaver Who Would Not Give Up
paras: In a small town in Kutch, Gujarat, a young weaver named Salim Hussain learned the craft of handloom weaving from his grandfather. The family had been making traditional shawls and rugs for generations, using patterns passed down through memory and practice. Salim loved the rhythm of the loom and the bright colours of the threads, but by the time he was twenty, machine-made cloth was flooding the market.

Cheap factory products were faster to produce and easier to sell. Many local weavers began to abandon their looms and search for other work. Salim’s income dropped sharply, and some relatives advised him to close the workshop. For a while, he felt discouraged and uncertain about the future of his family’s craft.

Instead of giving up, Salim decided to adapt. He travelled to nearby cities to understand what customers wanted and noticed a growing interest in handmade, eco-friendly products. He began experimenting with natural dyes made from plants and introduced new designs while keeping the traditional patterns alive. Each piece he created carried a small label telling the story of the weaver behind it.

Slowly, his work found new buyers. A craft fair in Ahmedabad brought him his first large order, and later a women’s cooperative helped him sell his products online. Salim also trained a group of young apprentices so that the skill would not disappear from his town.

Today, Salim’s workshop is busy once again. He often says that tradition does not survive by standing still; it survives when people respect the past but are willing to change with the times. His journey shows that perseverance, combined with creativity, can breathe new life into an old art.

reading.title: Lessons from a Beehive
paras: During a summer camp in Coorg, a group of students visited a small bee farm tucked away among coffee plantations. The farm belonged to Mr Joseph, a retired science teacher who had taken up beekeeping as a hobby. At first, the students were nervous about being so close to thousands of buzzing insects, but Mr Joseph’s calm manner soon put them at ease.

Wearing protective nets, the students watched as Mr Joseph gently lifted a wooden frame covered with bees. He explained that every beehive has a clear system of work. The queen bee lays eggs, the worker bees collect nectar and care for the young, and the drones have their own specific role. No bee works for itself alone; the survival of the hive depends on cooperation.

Mr Joseph also showed the students how bees communicate through movements known as the “waggle dance”. By dancing in a particular pattern, a bee can tell others where to find flowers rich in nectar. The students were amazed that such tiny creatures could share information so precisely.

Before the visit ended, Mr Joseph spoke about the importance of bees in nature. He explained that bees help pollinate many of the fruits and vegetables people eat every day. Without them, farming would become far more difficult and food would be less plentiful. He urged the students to protect flowering plants and avoid harming insects unnecessarily.

On the way back to camp, the students could not stop talking about what they had seen. The beehive had taught them more than a science lesson. It had shown them how discipline, teamwork and respect for nature could exist together in perfect balance.

reading.title: Green Corners at Home
paras: Plants do more than make a place look pleasant. They cool the air, provide shade, and give birds and insects a safe place to rest. In crowded neighbourhoods where open parks are few, even a small row of potted plants on a balcony can improve the surroundings. Recognising this, Maple Grove Society decided to encourage every household to create a small green corner at home.

The society began by organising a weekend workshop on easy-to-grow plants. Residents learned how to reuse old containers, prepare simple compost from kitchen waste, and water plants without wasting water. The organisers explained that gardening did not require a large yard; a sunny window, a balcony railing or a shared terrace could all be used wisely.

To measure the response, the residents’ committee conducted a survey at the end of two months. They counted how many saplings had been planted in each block of the society. The results were encouraging, especially in blocks where families had worked together and shared cuttings with their neighbours.

The committee noticed that the activity had benefits beyond greenery. Children became curious about how plants grow, elderly residents enjoyed spending time outdoors, and neighbours who had rarely spoken before began exchanging tips and seeds. The simple habit of caring for a plant brought people closer.

After reviewing the survey, the society decided to hold a monthly “Green Hour” where residents could exchange saplings and discuss plant care. The committee believed that when small efforts are made regularly, even a concrete neighbourhood can slowly become healthier and more welcoming.

reading.title: The Morning Fitness Drive
paras: Physical activity is essential for growing children, yet many students today spend long hours sitting in classrooms or looking at screens at home. To promote healthier habits, Riverdale Middle School introduced a “Morning Fitness Drive” for one month. For the first fifteen minutes of every school day, students took part in simple exercises such as stretching, skipping and brisk walking.

The physical education teachers explained that regular movement improves strength, posture and concentration. They also reminded students that fitness does not always require expensive equipment or special training. Small routines, when followed consistently, can have lasting benefits.

At the end of the month, the sports department recorded how many students from each house participated regularly in the drive. Participation meant attending the morning session on most school days. The data helped teachers understand which house groups were most enthusiastic and which ones needed more encouragement.

Students reported that the morning sessions made them feel more active and alert during the first period. Some even began practising the exercises at home with their family members. Teachers observed fewer complaints of tiredness and better attention in class.

Encouraged by the response, the school decided to continue the fitness drive twice a week throughout the term. The principal noted that good health habits formed early often stay with students for life, making such initiatives truly worthwhile.

reading.title: Saving Electricity at School
paras: Electricity makes modern school life possible, from lighting classrooms to running fans, computers and projectors. However, wasting electricity increases costs and puts pressure on natural resources. To build awareness, Hilltop Public School launched a month-long “Switch Off, Save On” campaign.

Student volunteers were appointed as “energy monitors” in every class. Their job was simple but important: to ensure that lights and fans were switched off when a room was empty, and that devices were not left on unnecessarily. Teachers supported the effort by discussing everyday habits that reduce power consumption.

The school maintenance team recorded the number of electricity units saved by each class compared to the previous month. The figures were displayed on a notice board so that students could see the results of their actions. Friendly competition among classes made the campaign more engaging.

By the end of the month, the school had saved a noticeable amount of electricity. Students learned that conservation is not about one grand action but about many small choices made every day. Turning off a fan for ten minutes may seem minor, but repeated across many classrooms, it makes a real difference.

Impressed by the outcome, the principal announced that the role of energy monitors would continue throughout the year. The campaign showed that students can play an active role in protecting resources when they are given responsibility and clear goals.

reading.title: A Week Without Plastic Bottles

Students were encouraged to bring water in reusable steel or copper bottles instead of buying disposable ones.

Before the week began, teachers explained how plastic waste often ends up in drains, rivers and open grounds. They discussed simple alternatives and asked families to support the effort at home. The aim was not to blame anyone, but to help students understand the impact of everyday choices.

Throughout the week, class representatives counted how many reusable bottles were brought each day in their sections. The eco-club compiled the data at the end of the week and presented it during the morning assembly. The numbers showed that participation improved steadily as more students remembered to carry their own bottles.

Many students said that once they developed the habit, it felt easy and practical. Some parents also reported that they had started carrying reusable bottles to work. The campaign sparked conversations about reducing waste in other areas, such as lunch packaging and shopping bags.

At the end of the week, the eco-club displayed a poster thanking everyone for their effort and reminding them to continue the practice. The school hoped that a small, focused campaign could lead to lasting change in daily behaviour.

reading.title: The Healthy Tiffin Survey
paras: A balanced diet helps students stay energetic, attentive and ready to learn. Yet many children either skip breakfast or bring snacks that are high in sugar and low in nutrition. To encourage better eating habits, Blossom Public School organised a “Healthy Tiffin Week” for Classes VI to VIII.

During the week, teachers spoke briefly about the value of fruits, vegetables, proteins and whole grains. The school canteen also displayed colourful charts showing simple, nutritious options that students could pack from home. The aim was not to criticise anyone’s food choices, but to help students understand how small changes can improve their daily health.

On Friday, class monitors conducted a survey to record the kinds of healthy items students had brought in their tiffins that day. Each monitor counted the items in their section and submitted the numbers to the activity coordinator. The results were later shared in the assembly so that everyone could see the overall response.

The survey showed that many students had made an effort to include wholesome food. Teachers noticed that discussions about nutrition became more lively, and some students even exchanged ideas for easy recipes that could be prepared quickly in the morning. Parents, too, appreciated the practical suggestions shared by the school.

Pleased with the participation, the school decided to repeat the activity once every month. The coordinator remarked that healthy habits grow stronger when students learn about them in a friendly and supportive environment rather than through strict rules alone.

questions.prompt: State whether the verb is transitive or intransitive: “I feel a severe pain in my leg.”
questions.why: “A severe pain” is the direct object.

questions.prompt: State whether the verb is transitive or intransitive: “We talked about the incident.”
questions.why: No object; “about the incident” is a prepositional phrase.

questions.prompt: Identify the objects: “The principal promised me a scholarship.”
questions.why: To whom? me (indirect). What? a scholarship (direct).

questions.prompt: Identify the complement: “We felt cold.”
questions.why: “Cold” describes the subject.

questions.prompt: Identify the complement: “We named the child Sita.”
questions.why: “Sita” refers to the object “the child”.

questions.prompt: Identify the complement: “The night grew cold.”
questions.why: “Cold” describes the subject “night”.

questions.prompt: Identify the complement: “The committee found him guilty.”
questions.why: “Guilty” describes the object “him”.

questions.prompt: Identify the complement: “The pill tastes bitter.”
questions.why: “Bitter” describes the subject.

questions.prompt: Identify the complement: “Exercise has made him sturdy.”
questions.why: “Sturdy” describes the object “him”.

questions.prompt: Identify the complement: “His account filled us with amazement.”
questions.why: The answer key marks “with amazement” as the objective complement.

grammar.title: G-05 Adjectives
grammar.meta: Ex A, C, D, E — 20 questions

questions.prompt: Identify the adjective of quality: “Ronit prepared a beautiful chart on the benefits of afforestation.”
questions.why: “Beautiful” describes the quality of the chart.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “enough” in “I have bought enough supplies to last me a week”?
questions.why: It indicates how much.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “Every” in “Every household in my locality has contributed generously”?
questions.why: It refers to each one of a number.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “Those” in “Those sweets in the third row are made from dry fruits”?
questions.why: It points out which sweets.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “Which” in “Which fruit is your favourite?”
questions.why: Used with a noun to ask a question.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “their” in “I visited their house while I was passing through the city”?
questions.why: It shows possession.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “incessant” in “The incessant rains in Jaipur brought life to a standstill”?
questions.why: It describes the quality of the rains.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “scenic” in “an hour-long scenic cruise along the Mandovi River”?
questions.why: It describes the quality of the cruise.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “salted” in “The salted peanuts and the tangy chips were a treat”?
questions.why: It describes the quality of the peanuts.

questions.prompt: What kind of adjective is “red” in “My dress for the function will be a red sherwani”?
questions.why: Colour is an adjective of quality.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with the adjective form of “child”: “He behaved like a child.”
options: He childishly behaved like a child.
questions.why: Notes answer: He exhibited childish behaviour.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with the adjective form of “bluntness”: “He spoke with bluntness.”
options: He spoke in a blunt manner.
questions.why: Notes answer: He spoke in a blunt manner.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with the adjective form of “population”: “London is a city with a large population.”
options: London is a populated city largely.
questions.why: Notes answer: London is a populous city.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with the adjective form of “silence”: “You should maintain silence in the library.”
options: You should remain silent in the library.
You should silent in the library.
You should maintain silent in the library.
You should be silence in the library.
questions.why: Notes answer: You should remain silent in the library.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with the adjective form of “happily”: “The children are playing happily in the park.”
options: The happy children are playing in the park.
The children are happy playing happily.
The happily children are playing in the park.
The children played happy in the park.
questions.why: Notes answer: The happy children are playing in the park.

questions.prompt: Use the opposite of “sharp”: This ______ knife is useless.
questions.why: The notes answer is blunt.

questions.prompt: Use the opposite of “interesting”: I can not read further. This is a rather ______ story.
questions.why: The notes answer is dull.

questions.prompt: Use the opposite of “pleasing”: Turn off the radio. It is very ______.
questions.why: The notes answer is annoying.

questions.prompt: Complete the letter: “Sorry for not having written recently, but I haven't had ______ time.”
questions.why: “Time” is uncountable, so “much”.

questions.prompt: Complete the letter: “I have visited ______ cities during the month.”
questions.why: Plural countable “cities” takes “many”.

poemExtracts.label: Extract 1
text: My next-door neighbour, Mrs. Jones,
has got a garden full of stones:
A crazy path, a lily pond,
a rockery and, just beyond
A sundial with a strange device,
which Mrs. Jones thinks rather nice.
My next-door neighbour, Mrs. Jones,
puts little plants between the stones
They are so delicate and small,
they don't mean anything at all.
I can't think how she gets them in,
unless she plants them with a pin.

questions.q: What is Mrs. Jones’s garden mostly made of?
options: Stones, a rockery and a crazy path
questions.why: “has got a garden full of stones: / A crazy path, a lily pond, / a rockery” — stone is the material she builds with.

questions.q: “They don’t mean anything at all” shows that the speaker thinks the plants are
options: too small and ordinary to matter
questions.why: The plants are “so delicate and small” that the speaker cannot see the point of them — a judgement Mrs. Jones does not share.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The garden of stones, the sundial and the plants set “with a pin”: “A Concrete Example” by Reginald Arkell.

questions.q: What does the phrase “with a pin” add to the description?
options: It shows the plants were bought cheaply
It exaggerates how tiny the plants are
It proves Mrs. Jones sews her plants
It tells us the garden is dangerous
questions.why: The joke is hyperbole — the plants are so small that only a pin could set them in place.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means a heap of stones where small plants are grown?
questions.why: A rockery is a bank or heap of stones built to grow small alpine or trailing plants.

poemExtracts.label: Extract 2
text: My next-door neighbour, Mrs. Jones,
once asked me round to see her stones.
We stood and talked about a flower
for quite a quarter of an hour.
"Where is this lovely thing?" I cried.
"You're standing on it," she replied.

questions.q: How long did the speaker and Mrs. Jones talk about the flower?
questions.why: “We stood and talked about a flower / for quite a quarter of an hour” — fifteen minutes on something almost invisible.

questions.q: The conversation about the flower shows that the speaker
options: had seen the flower clearly all along
could not find the flower they were discussing
had never visited the garden before
questions.why: The speaker has to ask “Where is this lovely thing?” — the flower is so small that it cannot be seen.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The visit to see the stones and the flower the speaker was standing on: “A Concrete Example” by Reginald Arkell.

questions.q: The humour of the last line comes from
options: the surprise that the flower was under the speaker’s feet
the strange device on the sundial
questions.why: Situational irony: the speaker searches for the “lovely thing” while standing on it. The answer is the opposite of what is expected.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means the same as “beautiful”?
questions.why: “Where is this lovely thing?” — lovely is used here in the sense of beautiful or delightful.

poemExtracts.label: Extract 3
text: She stood at the crossing and waited long,
Alone, uncared for, amid the throng
Of human beings who passed her by
Nor heeded the glance of her anxious eyes.
Down the street, with laughter and shout,
Glad in the freedom of "school let out,"
Came the boys like a flock of sheep,
Hailing the snow piled white and deep.

questions.q: Where is the old woman standing?
options: On the steps of a church
questions.why: “She stood at the crossing and waited long” — she needs to get to the other side of the road.

questions.q: “Nor heeded the glance of her anxious eyes” means that the people
options: paid no attention to her worried look
asked her where she was going
questions.why: To heed is to pay attention; nobody noticed or cared about the fear in her eyes.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The old woman waiting “alone, uncared for” while the schoolboys stream past: “Somebody’s Mother” by Mary Dow Brine.

questions.q: “Came the boys like a flock of sheep” suggests that the boys
options: moved together in a careless, thoughtless crowd
were making a noise like animals
questions.why: The simile makes them a herd — moving as one, without stopping to think about the woman in their path.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means a large crowd?
questions.why: The “throng / Of human beings” is the crowd that passes her by.

poemExtracts.label: Extract 4
text: Her aged hand on his strong young arm
She placed, and so, without hurt or harm,
He guided the trembling feet along,
Proud that his own were firm and strong.
Then back again to his friends he went,
His young heart happy and well content.
"She's somebody's mother, boys, you know,
For all she's aged and poor and slow",

questions.q: Where did the old woman place her aged hand?
options: On the boy’s strong young arm
On the railings of the crossing
questions.why: “Her aged hand on his strong young arm / She placed” — she trusts his arm to carry her across.

questions.q: The boy was “proud that his own were firm and strong” because he was
options: glad that his strength could help someone
questions.why: His pride is not vanity — he is grateful that his firm feet can steady her trembling ones.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The boy’s arm, the “trembling feet” guided across and “She’s somebody’s mother”: “Somebody’s Mother” by Mary Dow Brine.

questions.q: “His young heart happy and well content” tells us that the boy
options: wanted a reward for his help
felt satisfied after helping the woman
was sorry he had missed the fun
was worried about being late home
questions.why: Content means satisfied — the good deed itself is his reward.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means led someone carefully?
questions.why: “He guided the trembling feet along” — to guide is to lead someone safely along a way.

poemExtracts.label: Extract 5
poemExtracts.poem: The Magic Brush of Dreams — Anonymous
text: Gopi sits beneath the banyan,
A twig is in her hand.
She sits there drawing pictures,
Pictures in the sand.
The winds blow by and sweeps away
The pictures in the sand.
But on a stone there sits a man,
A brush is in his hand.

questions.q: What is Gopi doing beneath the banyan tree?
options: Drawing pictures in the sand with a twig
questions.why: “A twig is in her hand. / She sits there drawing pictures, / Pictures in the sand.”

questions.q: What happens to Gopi’s pictures?
options: She sells them in the market
questions.why: “The winds blow by and sweeps away / The pictures in the sand” — her art lasts only until the next gust.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: Gopi drawing in the sand and the man with a brush on the stone: “The Magic Brush of Dreams”, a folk tale retold by an anonymous poet.

questions.q: The man sitting on the stone is important because he
options: is Gopi’s father looking for her
is about to give Gopi the magic brush
has come to buy her drawings
questions.why: The brush in his hand is the clue: in the next stanza he slips it into Gopi’s hand with his one condition.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means a small, thin branch?
questions.why: A twig is a small shoot or branch — Gopi uses it as a drawing stick.

poemExtracts.label: Extract 6
poemExtracts.poem: The Magic Brush of Dreams — Anonymous
text: She paints a muffler for a farmer,
A plough for another man,
A shawl for a grandmother,
And for a girl, a fan.
And soon the news spreads far and wide,
Through forests, fields, and plains,
Until the Zamindar himself
Hears of these magic gains.

questions.q: What does Gopi paint for the grandmother?
questions.why: “A shawl for a grandmother, / And for a girl, a fan” — each gift is matched to the person who needs it.

questions.q: “Through forests, fields, and plains” tells us that the news
options: travelled only to the next village
spread across a very wide area
was kept secret by the villagers
reached the Zamindar last of all
questions.why: The list of landscapes widens the map: the story of the brush travels far beyond Gopi’s own village.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The painted muffler, plough and shawl, and the news reaching the Zamindar: “The Magic Brush of Dreams”, a folk tale retold by an anonymous poet.

questions.q: The phrase “magic gains” suggests that the painted things
options: are sold to buy a plough
questions.why: Gains are things gained; the villagers gain real food, clothes and tools from paint.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means a wealthy landowner?
questions.why: The Zamindar is the rich landlord whose order sets the second half of the poem in motion.

poemExtracts.label: Extract 7
text: Queen of the gourd-flower, queen of the harvest,
Sweet and omnipotent mother, O Earth!
Thine is the plentiful bosom that feeds us,
Thine is the womb where our riches have birth.
We bring thee our love and our garlands for tribute,
With gifts of thy opulent giving we come;
O source of our manifold gladness, we hail thee,
We praise thee, O Prithvi, with cymbal and drum.

questions.q: Which power is being praised in this stanza?
questions.why: The stanza ends “We praise thee, O Prithvi, with cymbal and drum” — Prithvi is the earth.

questions.q: “Thine is the plentiful bosom that feeds us” means that the earth
questions.why: The earth is imagined as a mother whose “plentiful bosom” feeds all her children with her crops.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The women’s praise of Prithvi, “queen of the harvest”, with cymbal and drum: “Harvest Hymn” by Sarojini Naidu.

questions.q: The women praise the earth as the “source of our manifold gladness” because she
options: sends the rain that waters the fields
gives fertile soil that yields their crops
questions.why: Rain is Varuna’s gift and light is Surya’s; the earth’s own gift is fertility — “the womb where our riches have birth”.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means many and varied?
questions.why: Manifold means of many kinds — the earth is the source of many different kinds of joy.

poemExtracts.label: Extract 8
text: Lord of the Universe, Lord of our being,
Father eternal, ineffable Om!
Thou art the Seed and the Scythe of our harvests,
Thou art our Hands and our Heart and our Home.
We bring thee our lives and our labours for tribute,
Grant us thy succour, thy counsel, thy care.
O Life of all life and all blessing, we hail thee,
We praise thee, O Bramha, with cymbal and prayer.

questions.q: Which deity do all the voices praise in this stanza?
options: Bramha, the Lord of the Universe
questions.why: The last line names him: “We praise thee, O Bramha, with cymbal and prayer.”

questions.q: “Thou art the Seed and the Scythe” means that the divine is
options: the beginning and the end of the harvest
a farmer who works in the fields
the owner of the village land
both the rain and the sunlight
questions.why: The seed starts the crop and the scythe cuts it — God is pictured as both the source and the end of all growth.

questions.q: Identify the poem and the poet.
questions.why: The final chorus offering “our lives and our labours” to Bramha: “Harvest Hymn” by Sarojini Naidu.

questions.q: “We bring thee our lives and our labours for tribute” shows the speakers’
questions.why: They offer not just songs and garlands but their whole lives and work — the fullest kind of thanksgiving.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means help given in difficulty?
questions.why: Succour is aid or relief; counsel, which sits beside it, means advice.

proseExtracts.label: Extract 1
text: The Vijayanagara Empire was renowned for its glory, wealth, and cultural achievements. Among its many illustrious rulers, King Krishnadeva Raya (ruled 1509–29 CE) stood out as a wise and powerful monarch. His reign is often referred to as the Golden Era of the Vijayanagara Empire, a time when art, literature, and architecture flourished. A great patron of learning, Krishnadeva Raya was not only an eminent warrior but also a gifted poet.
His works, such as the epic Amuktamalyada and the Sanskrit drama Jambavati Parinayam, are acclaimed even today.

Krishnadeva Raya’s court was home to eight celebrated poets, collectively known as the Ashtadiggajas. These poets, including Allasani Peddana and Tenali Ramakrishna, enriched the literary tradition with their masterpieces.

questions.q: Whose reign is called the Golden Era of the Vijayanagara Empire?
questions.why: “His reign is often referred to as the Golden Era of the Vijayanagara Empire” — the pronoun refers to Krishnadeva Raya.

questions.q: Which two works of the king are named in the extract?
questions.why: The extract names “the epic Amuktamalyada and the Sanskrit drama Jambavati Parinayam”.

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: The Ashtadiggajas were eight celebrated poets in the king’s court.
questions.why: “Krishnadeva Raya’s court was home to eight celebrated poets, collectively known as the Ashtadiggajas.”

questions.q: Tenali Ramakrishna earned a special place in the court because of his
questions.why: He was “known for his quick wit and humour, earning him a special place in the king’s court as both a poet and a witty advisor.”

questions.q: Which word in the extract means “respected and famous”?
questions.why: Illustrious means respected and famous — the word used for the empire’s many rulers.

proseExtracts.label: Extract 2
text: Rama approached the throne, carrying a plateful of paddy seeds. Bowing low, he began, “Your Majesty, I bring you a revolutionary type of paddy seeds. If these are sown, the yield will be three times greater than the current results.”

One of the courtiers, known for his sarcasm, whispered just loud enough to be heard, “I wonder if these are magic seeds! Next, he’ll claim they grow without water.” Another muttered, “Perhaps he found them on the moon!” Snickers rippled through the court.
Rama smiled, unfazed. “That may be true, Your Majesty, but the real issue lies not with the seeds themselves but with the person who sows them.”

questions.q: What did Rama carry into the court?
questions.why: “Rama approached the throne, carrying a plateful of paddy seeds.”

questions.q: How much greater did Rama say the yield of his seeds would be?
questions.why: “If these are sown, the yield will be three times greater than the current results.”

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: The courtiers received Rama’s idea with serious admiration.
questions.why: They made sarcastic remarks about magic seeds and the moon, and “snickers rippled through the court” — mockery, not admiration.

questions.q: Why does Rama bring up a farmer who yawns while sowing?
options: To prove that seeds need special soil
To show the king that yawning is natural and not disrespect
To mock the courtiers who laughed
To ask for better irrigation for the empire
questions.why: The joke is a gentle trap: once the king accepts that yawning is “as natural as breathing”, he sees how unfairly he treated the queen.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means “not worried or disturbed”?
questions.why: Rama “smiled, unfazed” — he is not at all unsettled by the laughter and sarcasm around him.

proseExtracts.label: Extract 3
proseExtracts.source: The Case of the Fifth Word
text: Chief Brown would have liked to tell everyone about his only child. But who would believe him? Who would believe that the best detective alive was an eighth grader? So, he said nothing.

Encyclopedia never spoke of the help he gave his father. He didn’t want to seem different from other boys. But there was nothing he could do about his nickname. He was stuck with it. Only his parents and teachers called him by his real name, Leroy. Everyone else called him Encyclopedia.

questions.q: Why did Chief Brown say nothing about his son’s talent?
options: He was ashamed of his son
Nobody would believe that an eighth grader was the best detective
His son had asked him to keep it secret
The police department had forbidden it
questions.why: “Who would believe that the best detective alive was an eighth grader? So, he said nothing.”

questions.q: Why did Leroy never speak about the help he gave his father?
options: He was afraid of being punished
He did not want to seem different from other boys
He thought his father did all the work
questions.why: “He didn’t want to seem different from other boys” — his skill is kept quiet out of modesty.

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: Apart from his parents and teachers, everyone called Leroy “Encyclopedia”.
questions.why: “Only his parents and teachers called him by his real name, Leroy. Everyone else called him Encyclopedia.”

questions.q: What does “He was stuck with it” mean?
options: He could not get rid of the nickname
He had chosen the nickname himself
He was glued to his books
He could not remember his real name
questions.why: Being “stuck with” a name means it was fixed on him and he could do nothing about it.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means a familiar name given by friends?
questions.why: A nickname is a pet or familiar name — here, Encyclopedia instead of Leroy.

proseExtracts.label: Extract 4
proseExtracts.source: The Case of the Fifth Word
text: “Nolan and Davenport had met,” Chief Brown said, “while both were in prison in South Carolina. They became friendly because of shared interests.”
“Davenport came to live with Nolan a week before the jewellery store hold-up. During the hold-up, one gunman’s mask slipped. A clerk thought she recognised Nolan. But she wasn’t absolutely sure.”

“Nolan suffered from a bad heart for many years. Yesterday morning he had a stroke. He must have realised he was dying. With his last strength, he managed to put his will on the kitchen table. It leaves everything he owns, including his palm-tree nursery to Davenport.”

questions.q: Where had Nolan and Davenport met?
options: At the Diamond Mart on Sixth Avenue
questions.why: “Nolan and Davenport had met … while both were in prison in South Carolina.”

questions.q: What did Nolan’s will leave to Davenport?
options: Only a sheet from his desk calendar
Everything he owned, including the nursery
A share of the stolen jewellery
questions.why: The will “leaves everything he owns, including his palm-tree nursery to Davenport.”

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: The clerk was absolutely certain that Nolan was one of the gunmen.
questions.why: “A clerk thought she recognised Nolan. But she wasn’t absolutely sure” — her doubt is why Nolan was questioned but never arrested.

questions.q: Why did Nolan put his will on the kitchen table?
options: He wanted the police to find it quickly
He knew he was dying and wanted Davenport to inherit
He was hiding it from Davenport
He had no other paper in the house
questions.why: He had a stroke, “must have realised he was dying”, and used “his last strength” to leave everything to his old friend.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means a robbery carried out with threats or violence?
questions.why: A hold-up is a robbery conducted with the use of threat or violence — here, the raid on the Diamond Mart.

proseExtracts.label: Extract 5
text: Imagine building a bridge without the use of cement, stones, concrete, etc. Is it possible? The living root bridges are incredible feats of engineering built by the indigenous people of Meghalaya.

Crossing the many waterways without bridges was difficult for people in the past, during monsoons. Attempts to use bamboo or wooden bridges across these waterways proved futile as these bridges could not last long in the heavy rains and strong waters. Living root bridges are an innovative and indigenous solution to solve this age-old problem.

They are made of intertwined roots which are a sort of magic, but they aren’t imaginary. These bridges have been built for centuries by the indigenous people of the land. It is a naturally built ecosystem of local flora. It also symbolises the relationship and knowledge that the local people have over their region and the cultural significance that it holds for them.

questions.q: Who built the living root bridges?
questions.why: They are “incredible feats of engineering built by the indigenous people of Meghalaya”.

questions.q: Why did bamboo and wooden bridges prove useless in Meghalaya?
options: They were too expensive to build
They could not last in the heavy rains and strong waters
The local people did not know how to build them
They were too narrow for animals
questions.why: Such attempts “proved futile as these bridges could not last long in the heavy rains and strong waters.”

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: The living root bridges are only imaginary structures.
questions.why: “They are made of intertwined roots which are a sort of magic, but they aren’t imaginary” — they are real bridges, alive and growing.

questions.q: What do the root bridges symbolise, according to the extract?
options: The wealth of the Meghalaya government
The local people’s knowledge of their region and its cultural value
questions.why: They symbolise “the relationship and knowledge that the local people have over their region and the cultural significance that it holds for them.”

questions.q: Which word in the extract means “useless”?
questions.why: “Attempts … proved futile” — futile means having no useful result.

proseExtracts.label: Extract 6
text: This happens in Odisha. It is a beach in the Balasore district where one can witness the sea disappearing mysteriously—the Chandipur Beach which is known for its unique feature of playing hide-and-seek with its visitors.

The sea can actually be witnessed disappearing and reappearing. This is because the sea water moves. It retreats by 2–5 km during ebb tide, the duration between the high tide and low tide, and comes back to the shore at the time of high tide. This unusual natural phenomenon keeps on happening daily, where one can actually see the sea, and then watch it disappear in front of their eyes!

questions.q: In which district is the beach where the sea disappears?
questions.why: The Chandipur Beach lies “in the Balasore district” of Odisha.

questions.q: How far does the sea retreat during the ebb tide?
questions.why: “It retreats by 2–5 km during ebb tide” — kilometres, not metres.

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: The sea at Chandipur disappears only once a year.
questions.why: “This unusual natural phenomenon keeps on happening daily” — the sea hides and returns every single day.

questions.q: The phrase “playing hide-and-seek with its visitors” shows that the sea
options: seems to hide and then come back like a game
is full of fish and crabs
questions.why: The sea vanishes for kilometres and then returns — as if it were playing a game of hide-and-seek.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means “goes backwards”?
questions.why: To retreat is to move back — the water goes back from the shore during the ebb tide.

proseExtracts.label: Extract 7
text: “Nothing is lucky if you put it away. If you want luck, you must put it to some use.” “What can I do with a seed?” “Plant it.”
So Rakesh found a small space and began to dig up a flowerbed. “Hey, not there,” said Grandfather. “I’ve sown mustard in that bed. Plant it in that shady corner, where it won’t be disturbed.”
Rakesh went to a corner of the garden where the earth was soft and yielding. He did not have to dig. He pressed the seed into the soil with his thumb and it went right in.

questions.q: What had Grandfather already sown in the flowerbed Rakesh first chose?
questions.why: “I’ve sown mustard in that bed” — so the cherry seed had to go elsewhere.

questions.q: How did Rakesh plant the cherry seed?
options: He buried it deep in a pot
He pressed it into the soil with his thumb
He tied it to a twig
He gave it to his grandfather to plant
questions.why: “He pressed the seed into the soil with his thumb and it went right in.”

questions.q: State whether the following statement is true or false: Rakesh planted the cherry seed in an open, sunny flowerbed.
questions.why: Grandfather sent him to “that shady corner, where it won’t be disturbed” — not an open, sunny bed.

questions.q: What does Grandfather’s advice about luck tell us about him?
options: He believes luck comes from putting things to use, not saving them
He thinks cherry seeds are worthless
He does not believe in luck at all
He wants Rakesh to sell the seed
questions.why: “Nothing is lucky if you put it away. If you want luck, you must put it to some use” — luck must be turned into effort.

questions.q: Which word in the extract means “giving way under pressure”?
questions.why: The earth was “soft and yielding” — it gave way under his thumb, so he did not have to dig.

proseExtracts.label: Extract 8
text: It was about two feet high when a goat entered the garden and ate all the leaves. Only the main stem and two thin branches remained.
“Never mind,” said Grandfather, seeing that Rakesh was upset. “It will grow again, cherry trees are tough.”

Towards the end of the rainy season new leaves appeared on the tree. Then a woman cutting grass scrambled down the hillside, her scythe swishing through the heavy monsoon foliage. text: In 1945, Bibha’s academic journey took her to the University of Manchester. Under the guidance of the celebrated Nobel Laureate, Patrick M.S.
